sutta: Okay, today's uh 28th of July. Continue with the Nidana Samyutta. We come to Sutta 12.67. On one occasion, the venerable Sariputta and the venerable Mahakassapa were dwelling at Varanasi in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then in the evening, the venerable Mahakassapa emerged from seclusion and approached the venerable Sariputta. They exchanged greetings with the venerable Sariputta. And when And when they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side and said to him, "How is it, friend How is it, friend Sariputta, is aging and death created by oneself, or is it created by another, or is it created both by oneself and by another, or has it arisen or has it arisen fortuitously, being created neither by oneself nor by another?" "Friend Gotama, aging and death is not created by oneself, nor is it created by another, nor is it created both by oneself and another, nor has it arisen fortuitously, being created either neither by oneself nor another, but rather with birth as condition, aging and death comes to be. This fortuitously is the by chance. How is it How is it, friend Sariputta, is birth created by oneself, is existence, clinging, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name and nama-rupa, mentality and materiality, are created by oneself, or is it created by another, or is it created both by oneself and by another, or has it arisen fortuitously, being created neither by oneself nor by another? Mentality and materiality, friend Gotama, is not created by oneself, nor is it created by another, or is created both by oneself and by another, or has it arisen fortuitously? Fortuitously being created neither by oneself nor by another, but rather with consciousness as condition, mentality and materiality comes to be. How is it, friend Sariputta, is consciousness created by oneself, or is it created by another, or is it created both by oneself and by another, or has it arisen fortuitously being created neither by oneself nor by another? Consciousness, friend Gotama, is neither created by oneself nor is it created by another, nor is it created both by oneself and by another, nor has it arisen fortuitously being created neither by oneself nor by another, but rather with mentality and materiality as condition, consciousness comes to be. Now we understand the Venerable Sariputta's statement thus: Mentality and materiality, friend Gotama, is not created by oneself, but rather with consciousness as condition, mentality and materiality comes to be. Now we also understand the Venerable Sariputta's other statement thus: Consciousness, friend Gotama, is not created by oneself, etc., but rather with mentality and materiality as condition, consciousness comes to be. But how, friend Sariputta, should the meaning of this statement be seen? Well then, friend, I will make up a simile for you, for some intelligent people here understand the meaning of the statement by means of a simile. Just as two sheaves of reeds must stand leaning against each other, so too, with mentality and materiality as condition, consciousness comes to be. With consciousness as condition, mentality and materiality comes to be. With mentality and materiality as condition, the six sense bases come to be. With the six sense bases as condition, contact, etc. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. Reverend Sariputta continued, "If friend, one were to remove one of those sheaves of reeds, the other would fall. And if one were to remove the other sheaf, the first would fall. So too with the cessation of mentality and materiality comes cessation of consciousness. With the cessation of consciousness comes cessation of mentality and materiality. With the cessation of mentality and materiality comes cessation of the six sense bases. With the cessation of the six six sense bases, cessation of contact, etc. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering." Let's stop here for a moment. So here, Reverend Sariputta is trying to explain that mentality and materiality and consciousness, they are a pair. They arise together and cease together. Now they stand supporting each other. So when one of them falls, the other also falls. They cannot one cannot exist without the other. So that's why he says in one place he says, "Consciousness conditions mentality and materiality." And on the other hand, he also says that "Mentality and materiality conditions consciousness." So you can say it in either way. Although the Patichchasamuppada, the formula of dependent origination, I say that consciousness conditions mentality and materiality. But as said here, you can also say that mentality and materiality conditions consciousness. Venerable Anuruddha said, "It is wonderful, friend Sariputta. It is amazing, friend Sariputta. How well this has been stated by the Venerable Sariputta. Rejoice in the Venerable Sariputta's statement on these 36 grounds. If friend among teaches the Dhamma for the purpose of revulsion towards aging and death, towards fading away and cessation, he can be called a monk who is a speaker on the Dhamma. If a monk is practicing for the purpose of revulsion towards aging and death, towards fading away and cessation, he can be called a monk who is practicing in accordance with the Dhamma. If through revulsion towards aging and death, towards fading away and cessation, a monk is liberated by non-clinging, he can be called a monk who has attained Nibanna in this very life. Similarly, if if friend among teaches the Dhamma for the purpose of revulsion towards birth or existence of clinging, craving, feeling, contacts, six sense bases, mentality and materiality, consciousness, volition, ignorance, towards fading away and cessation, he can be called a monk who is a speaker on the Dhamma. If a monk is practicing for the purpose of revulsion towards ignorance, towards fading away and cessation, he can be called a monk who is practicing in accordance with the Dhamma. If through revulsion towards ignorance, towards fading away and cessation, a monk is liberated by non-clinging, he can be called a monk who has attained Nibanna in this very life. It's the end of the sutta. So, in this second part, the venerable Sariputta says that uh venerable uh venerable Mahakottitha said that the venerable Sariputta's statement uh he rejoices on 36 grounds. What is this 36 grounds? Uh 36 reasons uh according to the comment to the commentary uh obtained by taking three cases in relation to each of the 12 terms. The first is the quality of being a speaker on the Dhamma. The second is the practice of the Dhamma. The third is the fruit of the practice of the Dhamma. So, three times uh 12 because there are 12 links. So, you get 36. Now, here you see how it says uh if a monk teaches the Dhamma for the purpose of revulsion towards aging and death or for the purpose of revulsion towards any one of these 12 links, uh then he is uh really called a speaker of the Dhamma. So, the purpose of speaking the Dhamma is to teach people to have revulsion towards these uh conditions that give rise to suffering for letting go of the worldly pleasures, uh letting go of the round of rebirth, and then if a monk is practicing for the purpose of revulsion towards uh suffering uh or any of the conditions giving rise to suffering, uh then he is called a monk who is practicing practicing in accordance with the Dhamma. Mhm. And if a person has already achieved revulsion towards suffering and all that, then he's liberated. So, here a real speaker of the Dhamma is one who teaches people to have revulsion towards suffering and all the conditions for suffering. And nowadays, sometimes uh you get people who speak on the Dhamma and they speak on a lot about worldly Dhamma. It's nothing to do with uh the Buddha's teachings. So, that is not called a speaker of the Dhamma. Next sutta is 12.68. On one occasion, the Venerable Mūsīla, the Venerable Saviṭṭha, and the Venerable Nārada, and the Venerable Ānanda were living at Kosambī in Ghosita's Park. Then the Venerable Saviṭṭha said to the verbal Musila, "Friend Musila, apart from faith, apart from personal preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reason reflection, apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, does the verbal Musila have personal knowledge that with birth as condition, aging and death comes to be?" And he said, "Friend Savita, apart from faith, apart from personal preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reason reflection, apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, I know this, I see this with birth as condition, aging and death comes to be." Again, he asked, "Friend Musila, apart from faith, apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, does the verbal Musila have personal knowledge that with existence as condition, birth etc., etc., with ignorance as condition, volition?" And he replied, "Friend Savita, apart from faith, etc., apart from acceptance of a view, I know this, I see this with ignorance as condition, volition." Again, verbal Savita asked, "Friend Musila, apart from faith, etc., apart from acceptance of a view, does the verbal Musila have personal knowledge that with the cessation of birth comes cessation of aging and death? etc., with the cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volition." And he replies, "Friend Savita, apart from faith, etc., I know this, I see this with the cessation of birth comes cessation of aging and death. etc., with the cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volition." "Friend Musila, apart from faith, apart from personal preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reason reflection, apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, does the verbal Musila have personal knowledge that Nirvana is a cessation of existence?" And he replied, "Friend Savita, apart from faith, apart from personal preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reason, reflection, apart from acceptance of a view of a pondering, I know this, I see this, Nirvana is a cessation of existence." And then venerable Savita said, "Then the venerable Musila is an Arahan, one whose asavas are destroyed." When this was said, the venerable Musila kept silent. Let me stop here for a moment now. So, here you see, venerable Savita is asking a series of questions to test the venerable Musila whether he's an Arahan. So, venerable Musila answered that he has personal experience of all these states, which implies that he's an Arahan. So, when venerable Savita said that venerable Musila must be an Arahan, he kept silent. And he kept silent, it means that then he is an Arahan. So, when he's an Arahan, he won't he won't boast that he's an Arahan. But if you were not an Arahan, then you would have to deny it. Since he kept silent, that means he he's implying that he's an Arahan. Then the venerable Narada said to the venerable Savita, "Friend Savita, it would be good if I if I asked that series of if I were asked that series of questions, ask me that series of questions and I will answer you." So, the venerable Narada here is inviting venerable Savita to ask him the same questions. So, venerable Savita asked venerable Narada the same series of questions and he received the same replies as venerable Musila gave. And venerable Savita said, "Then the venerable Narada is an Arahan, one whose asavas are destroyed." And venerable Narada replied, "Friend, though I have clearly seen as it really is with correct wisdom, Nibanna is the cessation of existence. I am not an Arahan, one whose asavas are destroyed. Suppose, friend, there was a well along a desert road, but it had neither a rope nor a bucket. Then a man would come along, oppressed and afflicted by the heat, tired, parched, and thirsty. He would look down into the well, and the knowledge would occur to him there is water, but he would not be able to make bodily contact with it. So too, friend, though I have clearly seen as it really is with correct wisdom, Nibanna is the cessation of existence. I am not an Arahan, one whose asavas are destroyed." When this was said, venerable Ananda asked venerable Savita, "When he speaks in such a way, friend Savita, what would you say about venerable Narada?" "When he speaks in such a way, friend Ananda, I would not say anything about venerable Narada except what is good and favorable." That's the end of the sutta. So here, venerable Narada, although he says he's not an Arahan, but he has seen with wisdom Nibanna as the cessation of existence and the other conditions. So it means that he is an Anagamin, has attained the third fruit. The only thing is it's like this person, he has seen the water, but he cannot touch the water. Meaning that the Arahan can see the water and can touch the water. So that's the difference that he sees all these states, and yet he has not achieved the final condition. That the difference between an Anagamin and the Arahan is that the Arahan has destroyed the five higher fetters. Five higher fetters and let me see um it's attachment to the form existence, attachment to the formless existence conceit conceit is the ego la. Restlessness la. And ignorance la. So, this uh Anagami now he has seen the the Dhamma clearly and and yet not he still has the self la. So, he's hasn't finished his work la. On that occasion the Blessed One was honored, respected, esteemed, venerated and revered. He obtained robes, alms food, lodgings and medicinal requisites. The bhikkhu sangha too was honored, respected, esteemed, venerated and revered. And the bhikkhus or the monks too obtained robes, alms food, lodgings and medicinal requisites. But the wanderers of other sects were not honored, respected, esteemed, venerated and revered. And they did not obtain robes, alms food, lodgings and medicinal requisites. Now, on that occasion the wanderer Susima was residing in Rajagaha along with a large company of wanderers. Then his company said to the wanderer Susima, "Come, friends, Susima, lead the holy life under the ascetic Gotama. Master his Dhamma and teach it to us. We will master his Dhamma and preach it to the lay people. Thus, we too will be honored, respected, esteemed, venerated and revered. And we too will obtain robes, arms, food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites. All right, friends, the wanderer Susima replied. He then approached the venerable Ananda and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side and said to him, friend Ananda, I wish to lead the holy life in this Dhamma-Vinaya. Then the venerable Ananda took the wanderer Susima approach and approached the Blessed One. He paid homage to the Blessed One, and then he sat down to one side and said to him, venerable sir, this wanderer Susima says that he wishes to lead the holy life in this Dhamma-Vinaya. Well, then Ananda, give him the going forth. The wanderer Susima then received the going forth and the higher ordination under the Blessed One. Stop here for a moment. So, you see this uh external sect wanderers, they saw that the Buddha and his disciples were getting a lot of offerings. Whereas they were getting very few offerings. So, they asked Susima to go and learn the Dhamma. On that occasion, a number of monks had declared final knowledge in the presence of the Blessed One saying, we understand destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. The venerable Susima heard about this. "Yes, friend." They replied. And then he said, "Then knowing and seeing thus, do you verbal ones wield various kinds of spiritual psychic power, such that having been one, you become many. I mean, one body, you multiply into many bodies. Having been many, you become one. You appear and vanish.
